spectrum.core: The entire Journey to the West is a metaphor for Daoist inner-alchemy and Buddhist mind-nature study — Sun Wukong is the ‘monkey mind’ and Bajie the ‘horse of intent’; the pilgrimage west is a course of self-cultivation, the eighty-one ordeals are the trials of practice, and the final attainment is the realization of one’s true mind.
spectrum.havoc: Havoc in Heaven = the untamed monkey mind running wild with delusion; it must be suppressed by the Five Elements Mountain (precepts, concentration, wisdom) before one can turn to the true path of self-cultivation. An untamed mind, however great its powers, is still a demon.

spectrum.core: Journey to the West is the pinnacle of the gods-and-demons novel — ‘gods and demons all have human feelings, spirits and monsters all understand the ways of the world’; the author writes with a playful brush about worldly hearts, not necessarily pointing to anything, nor necessarily pointing to nothing — literariness precedes allegory.
spectrum.havoc: Havoc in Heaven = the ultimate eruption of literary imagination, a heroic narrative of resistance against authority, the most resplendent movement in the whole book — no need to force a Daoist alchemical allegory.

spectrum.core: Journey to the West is a history of disciplined rebellion — Sun Wukong’s fall from Great Sage Equal to Heaven to the Victorious Fighting Buddha is the tragedy of a hero absorbed by the system. Reading it again five hundred years later, what we want is not enlightenment, but one more rampage.
spectrum.havoc: Havoc in Heaven = the hero’s freest moment, and the beginning of his destined suppression. The journey west is freedom’s funeral; the tightening golden band is the system’s seal.
